summary: This memo explains how protocol standards were adopted for the ARPA Internet and the DARPA research community. It covers the process, the authority, and the relationship between the DARPA and DDN communities. It is a policy statement.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 902 explains how protocols became official standards for the ARPA-Internet and the DARPA research community. It also distinguishes that process from the separate authority that set policy for the Defense Data Network.

subtitle: How the ARPA-Internet research community adopted official protocol standards.

tldr.problem: The ARPA-Internet and Department of Defense networks had related but distinct authorities and processes for adopting protocol standards.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains a typical path from proposal and review through limited testing, revision, and designation as an official protocol.
tldr.outcome: It assigns standards authority for the DARPA research community to DARPA and the ICCB, and describes the separate DDN-PMO role for DDN.

sections.title: Two Communities, Two Authorities
sections.content:
The memo explains standards adoption for the ARPA-Internet and DARPA research community, and describes how that community related to the Defense Data Network (DDN). DARPA sponsored research and delegated aspects of Internet program management to the Internet Configuration Control Board (ICCB).

The DDN served Department of Defense operational use. Its Program Management Office set policy for DDN facilities and enforced standards adopted for DDN networks.
sections.plainLanguage: DARPA and the DDN had different roles in protocol policy. The ICCB helped manage the DARPA Internet program, while the DDN office set policy for DDN facilities.

sections.title: From Discussion to an Official Protocol
sections.content:
A typical protocol effort began with discussion, followed by a written draft circulated to interested people for revision. A stabilized proposal could be issued as an RFC describing a draft protocol, after which limited test implementations might be tried.

If the tests revealed problems, the protocol could be revised before wider implementation. If no problems arose, a new RFC could provide the complete definition and identify the protocol as official. The memo notes that actual cases often made exceptions to this typical path.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal was discussed, written down, reviewed, and sometimes tested with a small group. A later RFC could make the protocol official after revisions and testing.

sections.title: How DARPA and DDN Policies Related
sections.content:
The ICCB could select a protocol for the ARPA-Internet and develop an implementation plan. The DDN-PMO considered the matter separately: it could use the same schedule, wait for experimental results, or decide that the protocol was not required for DDN.

For the DARPA research community, DARPA delegated standards authority to the ICCB, which delegated day-to-day administration to the Deputy Internet Architect. For the Department of Defense generally, the memo identifies the Protocol Standard Steering Group and the DDN-PMO as the corresponding authorities.
sections.plainLanguage: A decision for the ARPA-Internet did not automatically set the DDN schedule. Each community had its own authority to decide which protocols it required.
